text:
US stock markets edge lower as future of AI development in question

Michael Race

Business reporter in Washington DC

US stock markets closed in negative territory for the second day in a row as uncertainty over a potential slowdown of AI development.

All three main indexes were down at the end of trading on Tuesday, though the declines were minimal.

Investors are weighing up whether calls of a slowdown and regulation from AI industry leaders will prompt government action, though recent comments from US President Donald Trump suggest an intervention is not in the works anytime soon.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google working together on AI safety efforts

Kali Hays

US technology reporter

An OpenAI executive, Chris Lehane, said during a Tuesday press briefing in Washington DC that the company was working on safety efforts alongside other major developers of AI tools, including rival Anthropic and Google.

"It's better to try to work together to prioritize safety," Lehane said, according to a report by Bloomberg.

While Lehane did not specify what talks between the companies entailed, he said they had started several weeks ago, before concerns about the potential risks of AI reemerged last week.

OpenAI chief to speak after welcoming calls for regulation

After hearing from Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman will address the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco a little later on.

When he's handed the microphone, we can expect him to follow Amodei and call for regulation of AI industries, rather than taking Huang's line that no new laws are needed - stay tuned for what he says at around 18:30 EDT (23:30 BST).

That's after Altman penned a lengthy social media post in recent days, in which he said his organisation welcomes a "federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI".

Though he said AI companies don't need to wait for legislation to start providing safety confidence, Altman said "consistent rules" to manage risk and "maximise benefits" are a good idea.

At OpenAI, he wrote, his teams already conducts safety work before releasing new AI models.

He stressed that progress on AI development "has been rapid and will continue to be", but accepted "it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs".

Pacing will be "well worth this cost", he added, stressing that "no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness", and suggesting companies will need government help for "international coordination".

"But first we should do what we can ourselves," he wrote.

Share prices in chip companies rebound after yesterday's spook

Michael Race

Business and economics reporter, Washington DC

Shares in some of the firms that manufacture the materials used to develop AI have rebounded from yesterday's losses.

While stock markets remain down overall, the share prices of Nvidia, Marvell Technology and Intel are all up so far today.

Why? Well, one reason could be investors responding to the latest remarks from US President Donald Trump, who has taken a different stance to those in the AI industry calling for a slowdown in development.

Trump has rejected such a move, claiming on Monday that fears about the safety of AI are a "hoax".

Whether there is a slowdown or not will impact the companies either in the AI development industry or supplying it.

Mere talk of a pause - which could lead to a fall in demand for materials such as microchips - spooked investors of major chipmakers yesterday.

A large chunk of the value of the US stock market is made up firms which are betting on the success of AI, which means whatever happens in this space will have financial implications across the world.

'Not our job to regulate AI' - Attorney General Todd Blanche says as he questions timing

We have just heard from US Attorney General Todd Blanche, who's been speaking with reporters at the White House.

Blanche was asked several questions about the US government's response to AI and growing calls for companies to slow down the pace of development.

He says if any laws are broken, his department will charge people but adds "I do not think it is the job of the Department of Justice to regulate; we are prosecutors not regulators".

He says AI is "extraordinarily beneficial to our society, there is a lot of great work that AI does", and questioned the timing of recent calls.

To talk about this as midterms approach, he says, is an effort to influence them.

"And that shouldn't be what drives the decisions we are making around AI. We can't lose the AI race to China. President Trump says that, everyone says that, they say it because it is true."

Businesses have 'responsibility to create a human-centric AI'

At the Salesforce conference, which has just seen addresses fromAnthropic boss Dario Amodei and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, the audience is hearing about AI's impact on jobs.

Denis Machuel, chief executive of human resources firm Adecco, says AI has been a boom for his company's recruiters and the candidates they work with.

"Recruiters saved 35 to 40% of their time thanks to agentic AI," he says.

Machuel says Adecco's vision is that AI has to "happen with people, not to people" and businesses have a "common responsibility to create a human-centric AI".

"People cannot be an after thought," he adds.

The conference's keynote speech has now ended - we'll continue to bring you lines as AI continues to be a debated topic in the US.

AI under discussion on both sides of America - what have we heard?

Debates continue in the US over the regulation of AI.

In Washington DC, Republican figure Steve Bannon and Democrat politician Bernie Sanders have been addressing the future of the tech:

Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders raised the alarm about artificial intelligence, telling the summit it "has has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs" and wipe out entire professions

As a result, he said, he will be introducing a bill next week to "permanently ban the development of artificial super intelligence”, and called on President Trump to negotiate a treaty on AI safety with China

Taking the stage after, Bannon said he and Sanders - unlikely partners - are "trying to raise above partisanship"

Trump's former White House adviser went on to accuse AI bosses of placing the risk of AI development on people, while "they want to keep all the upside"

Meanwhile in San Francisco Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang defended AI development:

Huang said "we don't need new laws or regulations" as he urged "companies to decide" on the safety of their tools

Amodei, though, admitted it is important to "invest more in safety" and pushed for an "international component" in setting these standards

It follows comments from Monday by an Anthropic executive, who told the BBC that AI is getting more powerful "by the day" and a kill switch should be mandatory.

Also on Monday, Donald Trump downplayed concerns, saying claims that it will take over the world are a "hoax"

'We don't need new laws,' Nvidia chief exec says of AI as he calls for self-regulation

Kali Hays

US technology reporter in San Francisco

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, says at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco that the development of AI did not call for any new rules to govern it.

"We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang says. "We need companies to decide... that innovation, speed, and safe products, that's a false choice."

Huang says that AI companies should be left to assess and act on the safety of their tools, and whether or not to release them.

He says that any company developing an AI tool should simply not release anything that they are not confident will be safe.

"Don't release it, that's a very obvious thing to do," Huang adds.

"Run as fast as you can, but if at any time you feel it's not in control, take a pause."

Important for AI industry to commit to standards and safety - Anthropic CEO

Kali Hays

US technology reporter in San Francisco

Over in San Francisco, Anthropic boss Dario Amodei has been speaking at an annual Salesforce conference, days after calling for the development of AI to slow down.

Asked about his remarks, Amodei says it is tempting to "attack" competitors but that it is more responsible to try and establish industry-wide standards.

"Let's make our practices better, let's recommit to transparency, let's invest more in safety, then let's organise the rest of the industry and say what can we do to set standards for everyone," he says, adding that there should be an "international component" to any such development.

"I think that's the way to lead the industry forward, to set an example, to say that everyone can always be better," he adds.

'We're trying to raise above partisanship,' says Bannon

Brandon Drenon

Reporting from Washington DC

Bannon finishes his speech by addressing the elephant in the room, which is the extremely unlikely situation unfolding where he is sharing the same stage at the same event as Bernie Sanders.

“I don't think you could find any two harder partisans than Bernie Sanders on the left and Steve Bannon on the right,” he says.

“We're trying to raise above partisanship, and we have to because this is a unique [moment].”

“This is a hinge in history,” Bannon continued. “They say this is a Cold War moment. This is like the nuclear age.”

We're now turning our attention over to the AI conference being held in California, where Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been speaking. We'll bring you his remarks next.

AI execs trying to 'use a crisis and turn it to their advantage' - Bannon

Brandon Drenon

Reporting from AI summit in Washington DC

Steve Bannon, Trump’s former White House adviser and known MAGA firebrand, entered the stage moments after Sanders and opened by reiterating his long-held belief that AI is “the defining issue of our time”.

Bannon repeatedly referred to AI tech executives as “the oligarchs” and said the statement over the weekend from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei – echoed by Elon Musk and OpenAI boss Sam Altman – was “a bald-faced lie”.

“They’ve tried to cover up the danger,” Bannon said, referring to AI special interest groups millions of dollars in investments into elections and what he categorised as disingenuous offerings by AI companies to self-regulate.

“What they want is to socialise all the risk with the American people, including potential bailouts, when they come,” he said. “And they want to keep all the upside.

“All they're trying to do is to use a crisis and turn it to their advantage.”

Sanders calls on US and China to work together on AI regulation

Brandon Drenon

Reporting from Washington DC

Sanders continues his speech, warning that if AI were to surpass human intelligence, as experts predict, it would bring “potentially catastrophic consequences”.

He says he will introduce a bill next week to “permanently ban the development of artificial super intelligence”.

“Further, this legislation will put an immediate pause on advanced AI development until we have clear safety rules in place developed by the most knowledgeable scientists in our country,” Sanders says.

He then calls on President Trump to negotiate a treaty on AI safety with China's President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Washington next week “to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on superintelligence”.

“A super intelligent AI that escapes human control will not simply be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem," he says. "It will be humanity's problem.”

On the other side of the country, conference attendees to hear from top AI bosses

While Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon address an AI summit in Washington DC, on the other side of the US, a conference is this morning expecting to hear from some of the most significant figures in AI.

At the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, there'll soon be an appearance from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as well as Anthropic boss Dario Amodei.

We're keeping an eye on proceedings, and we'll bring you anything they have to say on AI - and safety - as soon as we hear from the pair.

Sanders sends stark warning about risks posed by AI

Brandon Drenon

Reporting from AI summit in Washington DC

I'm here at the AI summit in Washington where Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has been raising the alarm about AI risks to the highest level.

He is among the progressive US lawmakers, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, calling for a complete moratorium on AI data centres.

“Let us be clear: artificial intelligence and robotics are the most transformational technologies in the history of humanity,” Sanders tells the crowd. “And they will impact the lives of every man, woman, and child in our country.”

“The economic impact of that is that AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for our young people to enter the workforce,” he continues.

“Civil libertarians warn us that AI is in the process of eviscerating our privacy rights by making it easier to collect and analyse every email that we send, every text, every website visit, and every trip that we make in our call, resulting in the creation of a mass surveillance state.”

A rare moment of bipartisanship in Washington

Daniel Bush

Washington correspondent

The growing backlash to AI is one of those rarest of things in hyper-partisan Washington: an issue with some semblance of bipartisan consensus.

Evidence of that comes today, as progressive Senator Bernie Sanders and conservative Steve Bannon are appearing at a forum in Washington on regulating the AI industry.

Their presence underscores how the right and left are uniting around an issue that's become a key talking point ahead of the elections in November.

One notable figure not on board with the bipartisan backlash is President Donald Trump.

Trump this week has argued that AI shouldn't be heavily regulated, a stance that may prove unpopular with voters across the political spectrum.

Silicon Valley tech firms alone shouldn't set safeguards, says Cohere CEO

Jessica Murphy

Reporting from investment summit in Toronto

In Toronto, where some AI executives, including representatives from OpenAI, are gathered for an investment summit hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney, the future of the tech is being pitched as bright.

Aidan Gomez, the CEO and co-founder of AI firm Cohere, said during a tech panel today that the weekend note by Anthropic's Dario Amodei calling for a slow down “was thought-provoking”.

But he cautioned that any time a sector or industry asks for rules like anti-trust protections, meant to prevent big firms from stifling competition, to be lifted should raise a “red flag”.

Still, AI is “the most sophisticated cyberweapon” the world has seen and that caution is warranted.

He said Silicon Valley tech firms alone shouldn't set safeguards around the rapidly developing technology, but they should be shaped by the public, the government and stakeholders, including industry.

Top AI bosses to speak publicly for first time since issuing warnings

Kali Hays

US technology reporter

An annual Salesforce conference in San Francisco will see some timely guests appearing on stage, including Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, Anthropic boss Dario Amodei, and OpenAI boss Sam Altman.

Each of the executives play a major role in the world of artificial intelligence and also a debate that was stirred up again last week over how safe the rapid development of AI tools is for the broader public and governments.

Today’s appearances will be the first time the executives have spoken publicly (outside of many X posts and blogs) since these concerns have reached a new pitch.

Former and current employees of Anthropic have recently gone public with concerns they say are widespread among people working on AI tools and projects that there is a small chance AI tools will become so capable in the not-too-distant future that the fate of humanity will be at risk.

While Amodei and Altman have regularly espoused the power of their companies’ tools, both are also planning in the coming months to list on the US stock market.

Huang, for his part, along with many other tech executives, have said that concerns that AI will “kill” humans are overblown.

Huang and Amodei are expected to appear at the San Francisco event sometime between 13:00 and 15:00 EDT (18:00 -20:00 BST), while Altman is slated to speak at 18:30 EDT

text:
Long regarded as the holy grail of AI research, AGI has for decades remained a goal somewhere over the horizon. And now, apparently, it’s here—at least, if Brockman is to be believed. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, another one of the industry’s most influential voices, seems convinced. He congratulated OpenAI on its achievement, tweeting, “AGI has arrived.”

There is, however, a problem with declaring that AGI has arrived: There is no universally accepted threshold for what counts as AGI, and many researchers would dispute that today’s models have crossed it. That ambiguity also gives companies plenty of room to claim the milestone early, especially when doing so carries obvious marketing value. It feels, in a sense, like the race among cellular carriers to slap the next “G” on their networks before the underlying technology fully satisfies the technical standard.

Now, Astra is an impressive model. It almost aced a benchmark test designed to resist attempts by model makers to train specifically for the test, which has been a major problem with AI benchmarks. The ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, developed by AI researcher François Chollet, tests a model’s ability to encounter a completely unfamiliar situation (in this case a series of video games), figure out how it works, learn to play efficiently, and win.

But Astra’s score depends heavily on the software used to administer the test. Running through OpenAI’s own “harness,” the software layer that lets the model interact with the benchmark, Astra scored 99.9%. Using ARC-AGI-3’s standard testing setup, designed to give models a more uniform interface, Astra scored 62.7%.

In any case, the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark doesn’t represent the finish line in the race for AGI, Chollet says, because it tests a non-exhaustive set of attributes at very small scales.

“The real world features much longer time horizons for continual learning compared to ARC 3 games (decades vs minutes), much larger world modeling complexity, much greater goal ambiguity, more greater exploration spaces, etc.,” Chollet says in an email to Fast Company.

text:
Big Chalk Analytics announced Tuesday subscription access to its Trade-Off Consumer database through a new web-based dashboard, giving CPG brands and retailers a way to track where consumers shop, what they buy and how they adjust spending as household budgets tighten.

One emerging shift points to a growing competitive threat for Walmart from Aldi. While 18% of Walmart shoppers say they are visiting Aldi more frequently, that rises to 24% among Walmart shoppers who are trade-off consumers. Nearly half (48%) of Walmart trade-off consumers already shop Aldi.

The data also offers a clue to Aldi’s appeal: 49% of Aldi trade-off consumers say they have switched to a less expensive or private-label brand in coffee. Together, the findings suggest Aldi is gaining traction with precisely the consumers most actively reconsidering brands, retailers and household spending.

“Walmart is still performing well with trade-off consumers, but Aldi is clearly finding ways to display value that are pulling at Walmart’s shopper base,” said Rick Miller, partner and Marketing Effectiveness Practice Lead at Big Chalk Analytics. “When 24% of Walmart trade-off consumers say they are increasing Aldi visits, versus 18% of Walmart shoppers overall, that is a competitive signal retailers and brands need to understand. The dashboard lets them identify who is shifting, then drill into the categories and trade-offs behind it.”

At the center of the data are the trade-off consumers—the roughly one-third of U.S. households actively cutting spending across categories through value-based trade-offs. With trended data dating to Spring 2024, the dashboard lets users track how these consumers are changing their behavior and compare them with the broader U.S. population and other shopper segments.

The Trade-Off Consumer Dashboard also enables clients to:

The dashboard can move from a retailer-level signal to the shopper segments driving it, then show how those consumers are changing brand choice, package size and category substitutions. That gives retailers and CPG brands a clearer view of threats and opportunities they can address through assortment, pricing, promotion and media.

“The trade-off consumer is not a temporary recession persona,” Miller added. “It is a durable shopping mindset representing roughly one-third of U.S. households. For companies fighting for share, understanding those trade-offs is becoming essential.”

text:
OpenAI has been engaging with other artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic and Google , about how they can work together to address safety concerns, a spokesperson confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday.

Discussions have been ongoing since Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, released a proposal in July calling for a U.S.-led "Standards Body," the spokesperson said. Hassabis published an essay on X where he suggested establishing a public-private partnership or self-regulatory organization with federal oversight, akin to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are fierce competitors, but the companies have been facing intense pressure to address mounting AI safety and security concerns in recent weeks. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI companies to slow how quickly they improve their most advanced models, a move that was lauded by Hassabis and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

"Dario's essay points towards the right path forward," Hassabis wrote in a post on X. "The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment."

Altman said he agrees with Amodei on the need to pace the industry's most advanced models. In a post on X, he said a slowdown has been a "primary topic" of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks, and that the company will have more to share "soon."

The Information earlier reported the discussions between the companies. Google and Anthropic did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Earlier this month, Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, published a blog post where he said OpenAI is working to advance "industry-led standards." He said the company will work with other companies to build out a voluntary effort, "with or without government support."

"Any industry-led standards would complement — not replace — mandatory federal safeguards and democratic oversight," Lehane said. "But we have entered a different phase of AI capabilities, and everything should be on the table — including considering what can be built voluntarily outside government as an immediate step."

text:
By bidding at their bankruptcy proceedings, she proposed, it might be possible to obtain detailed regulatory filings, manufacturing strategies, and safety data—types of information usually considered trade secrets. She called these documents “biotech’s lost archive” and said they could be used to help train AIs that would act as powerful copilots in the often opaque drug approval process.

Today the OpenAI Foundation, the nonprofit parent of OpenAI, said it would fund her idea as part of a new effort it calls Public Data for Health, which aims to help artificial intelligence make big leaps in medicine by paying to create “high-quality scientific datasets.”

The basic idea is that AI isn’t going to be capable of making important breakthroughs in curing disease unless researchers can feed the models much more information than they have so far.

“Everyone is recognizing that data is the biggest bottleneck in successfully applying AI to biology,” says Morgan Levine, a former vice president for computation at Altos Labs, a longevity company.

In its initial round of data grants, the OpenAI Foundation also announced that it would give $40 million to a program to collect data about novel cancer vaccines at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, and support OpenAdmet, a group that runs competitions in which researchers try to predict drug effects.

Teslo’s idea for a biotech archive received $500,000 and will be pursued by 1Day Sooner, an advocacy group representing clinical trial volunteers, which she advises.

“We expect many remaining breakthroughs in preventing and curing disease to come from pairing the intelligence of new models with more observations of the world—in other words, more data,” the OpenAI Foundation said in a statement.

OpenAI started as a nonprofit, but leader Sam Altman restructured it to form a for-profit corporation that develops new models, launches products, and is now planning an initial public offering of stock that could value it at $1 trillion.

Because the foundation holds a 26% equity stake in OpenAI, it is now be on track to become the richest charitable organization on the planet, potentially sitting on $250 billion in stock value. (By comparison, the Gates Foundation and a trust associated with it held about $180 billion at the end of 2025.)

Making good use of that kind of money will not be easy. The foundation, based in San Francisco, is still hiring for many key roles and started ramping up its grantmaking only this year. Its largest single gift so far, of $100 million, was awarded in August to the Common Health Coalition, an organization that helps patients get access to drugs for hepatitis C.

OpenAI’s charitable efforts come even as apocalyptic fears have broken out about the possibility that runaway AI could wipe out all human life, possibly by launching a deadly bioweapon.

Those fears have been stoked by AI company insiders, some of whom say the chance of human extinction within the next decade is 10% or more. Last week, Altman and xAI founder Elon Musk both endorsed a call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” so that risk prevention can catch up.

Jacob Trefethen, an executive at the foundation, says it essentially operates separately from OpenAI but shares an official mission of ensuring that artificial intelligence “benefits all of humanity.”

“We’re starting grantmaking when we think the best way to achieve that mission is to make grants to external nonprofits, research institutions, and other third parties,” Trefethen said in an interview. He says the foundation hopes to give away $1 billion by the end of the year.

The $500,000 grant to 1Day Sooner will help the group prove it can obtain the data troves of bankrupt companies, says the organization’s president and cofounder, Josh Morrison. He thinks nonexclusive copies of company datasets could be acquired for only “a few tens of thousands of dollars” each.

Morrison says two other attempts to obtain drug company files this year proved unsuccessful, after 1Day Sooner’s bids were not accepted.

Bankruptcies could become what some are calling a “new land grab” for AI training. Last month, Google won a bid to take over the corporate data of the failed carrier Spirit Airlines, including 100 million emails. That led to objections from flight attendants and others who worried that private or proprietary data could be exposed.

The drug company files that 1Day Sooner is seeking are known as common technical documents. They typically contain the back-and-forth between companies and regulators, as well as detailed scientific and medical measurements, and essentially provide everything that is known about a drug.

According to Teslo, who is a writer for Works In Progress and a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Progress, a think tank in Washington, DC, a stockpile of such files could help turn an AI into a regulatory expert, which in her view could be one of the main ways AI helps speed cures to market.

“People say ‘We will invent AI, and AI will cure cancer,’ but that’s very removed from the messy reality and the regulatory process,” she says. “About 70% of the money and time in drug development is spent in clinical development—organizing the trials and testing the drug—but despite that, the process is basically a black box, especially for small biotech companies generating the innovations.”

text:
(Alliance News) - The UK government is planning to take over Speciality Steel UK in a move set to cost around GBP350 million, after a private sector bid failed to secure its backing.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the government would work towards the "public acquisition" of the UK's third-largest steelworks.

Reynolds said a bidder had come forward to take over SSUK earlier this year, reported to be Norwegian firm Blastr Green Steel, but the government could not support it and was instead developing its own proposal.

Blastr said it was not told in advance about the government's decision and that it had developed a "fully-funded proposal at no cost to the British taxpayer".

SSUK was placed into the control of the state's Official Receiver last August, after it was forced to liquidate by the High Court.

Reynolds said he expected the process of bringing it into public ownership to take around four to six months.

He said the government would "have to pay off the creditors", acquire the assets and "inject some working capital over a period between one and three years".

The Business secretary continued: "I would anticipate the cost of that to be around GBP350 million."

Asked by Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper "where that money might come from", Reynolds replied the government had not yet spent "the lion's share" of GBP2.5 billion set aside for the steel industry, pledged in Labour's 2024 manifesto.

Reynolds said there was "nothing ideological" about the decision to acquire SSUK, adding: "I want this to be run in the private sector. That is my ideal."

Speciality Steel employs about 1,300 people, many of whom have been put on furlough with reduced wages.

Production at the business, which runs sites across Stocksbridge and Rotherham in South Yorkshire, and Wednesbury in the West Midlands, has been on pause in recent months.

Reynolds said the government had "serious concerns about the proposed financing" of a potential offer for SSUK.

Reynolds said: "We took a long, hard look at the offer that was on the table, but the truth is that we had serious concerns about the proposed financing of it, the protections for UK taxpayers, and whether it would be able to offer the long-term stability for the local economy and community."

The deal will "keep options open" for the business while working to determine the long-term future of its sites, he said.

A spokeswoman for Blastr Green Steel said: "We are disappointed by the government's decision today concerning Speciality Steel UK, and we were not informed in advance.

"Over the course of several months, we have advanced our plans for a private sector solution to acquire SSUK and were today on site in South Yorkshire with investors and strategic partners.

"We have a fully-funded proposal, at no cost to the British taxpayer, that is ready to complete within 12 weeks."

Trade unions said they welcomed the government's intervention after failing to find a credible buyer for SSUK.

Gareth Stace, UK Steel director-general, said: "This Government is once again stepping up to do what is needed for the UK steel industry.

"SSUK is already well on its way to returning to full operations and retaking its place at the heart of critical UK supply chains.

"It is crucial that the custodian of this key strategic asset is the right owner and investor, with the expertise and long-term ambition that the dedicated workforce deserve."

Roy Rickhuss, Community Union general secretary, said it was a "disappointing outcome" that a private sector buyer had not been secured, but that the government's intervention was a "welcome move".

"SSUK is a unique and integral component of the UK's steelmaking capabilities, without which we would be entirely reliant on foreign suppliers for high-value speciality inputs to our critical energy infrastructure and our advanced manufacturing base including the defence industries," he said.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said: "This government refuses to be a passive observer to the decline of our critical industries and the loss of good jobs. Inaction is not an option.

"Over the coming months, we will work with regional and local partners to agree a way forward that delivers for employees, the community and the country."

text:
As electricity demand surges and geopolitical risks persist, industry leaders argue that LNG’s value now extends beyond decarbonisation, becoming a cornerstone of energy security and reliable supply for an increasingly electrified world.

The rapid growth of electrification and artificial intelligence is transforming how governments and energy companies think about security of supply, with industry leaders warning that reliability is becoming as important as affordability and sustainability. Discussions during the “LNG in the Age of Electrification: Contracting, competition and demand realities” executive leadership panel session highlighted how geopolitical uncertainty, rising power demand, and the need for resilient energy systems are elevating LNG’s strategic role within the global energy mix.

Moderating the discussion, Carlos Pascual, SVP & Head – Geopolitics & International Affairs, S&P Global Energy, said electrification had become fundamental to economic growth, healthcare, education, mobility, and sustainability, while the rise of artificial intelligence was adding a new layer of urgency to energy planning. He said the combination of these forces had made electricity, gas, and LNG increasingly critical to national security.

For Dr Kongkrapan Intarajang, CEO & President of PTT, the lesson from recent years has been clear. Security and stability of supply are most important, he reiterated.

Thailand currently sources around 50% of its natural gas domestically and imports the remainder, making diversification a central part of its energy strategy. As the country prepares for growing demand from electrification and data centres, maintaining secure access to LNG has become increasingly important.

A recurring theme throughout the session was that security of supply can no longer be viewed as a short-term concern. Stephane Michel, President – Gas, Power & Renewables at TotalEnergies, whose company supplies around 10% of the global LNG market, argued that energy systems must balance affordability and reliability simultaneously.

“Security of supply will remain something that is absolutely key,” he said.

While debate over the role of different energy sources continues, Michel suggested the real challenge facing policymakers is not a choice between gas and renewable power, but rather that the competition is between gas and coal.

The panel also highlighted changing expectations among LNG buyers. Historically focused on efficiency and cost optimisation, customers are increasingly seeking flexibility and insurance against disruption.

Liz Westcott, CEO and Managing Director of Woodside Energy, which is expanding its portfolio across Australia and the US, said purchasing strategies have evolved significantly as supply risks have become more apparent.

“Customers have been looking to have just-in-time LNG. They’re now looking to think about: do we have just-in-case LNG?” Westcott said.

She added that portfolio diversity across regions and suppliers is becoming essential as buyers seek to manage exposure to geopolitical and market risks. Rather than replacing one energy source with another, many countries are pursuing broader energy expansion strategies.

The need for greater flexibility was echoed by other panellists. Resilience was a central theme for Mohamed Al Aryani, President – International Gas, XRG, who said customers increasingly want both long-term supply security and operational flexibility.

“Customers are telling us two things: they like long-term sustainable supply they can plan around, but they’d like flexibility they can manage around.”

The comments highlighted how the focus is shifting towards integrated value chains that connect production, trading, marketing, and power generation.

For utilities, the conversation is increasingly centred on power system reliability. Dr Narin Phoawanich, Governor of the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT), explained energy security today must be measured by the ability to deliver dependable electricity to consumers. “The security of supply is changing to reliable electricity supply,” he said.

As such, executives stress that infrastructure investment and long-term commercial relationships will be critical in meeting future demand. “We are living in a world where nothing is certain, so we need to plan for a lot of flexibility and adjustability,” Dr Intarajang said.

text:
Walmart and about 1,000 other merchants are asking a judge to reject final approval of a credit card fee settlement, arguing that it gives Visa, Mastercard and large banks “sweeping” immunity while offering merchants “temporary and meager relief.”

The largest U.S. retailer renewed its battle Monday against the settlement, asking a federal court to reject it, while joining with Circle K and the National Association of Convenience Stores in asking U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan to allow them to opt out and not be bound by the settlement, citing their constitutional rights.

“There has never been a mandatory (class action) settlement like this — one which would rework the payments system at the heart of the U.S. economy, based on speculative economic theory that has not even had the benefit of adversarial testing,” Walmart said in its 299-page legal broadside against the pact.

Walmart, Circle K and NACS said that forcing them to participate in the class unwillingly raises constitutional concerns under the Fifth Amendment’s “takings clause,” which prohibits the government from imposing economic disadvantage without proper compensation.

“NACS members are differently situated from other class members under the settlement specifically and are being treated inequitably by the settlement, warranting decertification if the settlement is approved and opt-out is not permitted,” the association and Circle K wrote Monday in their decertification motion.

Walmart has filed similar class decertification requests before, most recently in late 2025, which the court has declined. The latest request, if granted, would dissolve the group of about 12 million merchants designated as plaintiffs for the class action.

Merchants detail faults

Separately, a group of 29 merchants – including The Cigna Group, DoorDash, General Motors and Peet’s Coffee – also asked Cogan on Monday to reject the settlement, joining more than 900 merchants and trade associations that filed a similar objection on Thursday. They include the National Grocers Association, the National Restaurant Association and NATSO, the association that represents truck stops and travel centers.

In their filings, they called the settlement “inadequate” and said it “entrenches” the card networks’ “anticompetitive system of fees and rules.”

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Payments Dive free daily newsletter

Merchants and their trade groups who wanted to offer their views of the proposed settlement had until Monday to file their comments with Cogan, who is overseeing the multidistrict litigation in the Eastern District of New York.

Cogan gave the pact preliminary approval in June, and subsequently set a Nov. 16 hearing for arguments on whether the pact should be granted final approval. It’s possible that a decision on final approval may come by year’s end; Cogan ruled about six weeks after a hearing in April on the settlement’s merits.

The interchange fee litigation dates to 2005 and follows two prior settlements, both of which were nixed by courts, including the prior settlement proposal that was scotched in June 2024.

This proposed settlement would trim credit interchange fee rates by 0.1% for five years and impose a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards for eight years. It would also give merchants the right to decline some higher-cost Visa and Mastercard premium and commercial credit cards – a departure from the networks’ “honor all cards” rule.

In 2024, merchants paid a 2.35% fee on Visa and Mastercard transactions, according to a weighted average reported by the research organization Nilson Report last year.

Card swipe fees applied to transactions collectively have increased 80% since the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, to a record $198 billion last year, according to the Merchants Payments Coalition.

Changes under the pact

Merchants would also gain new rights to add surcharges and offer discounts for credit cards as a way to steer customers away from cards with higher interchange fees, under terms of the agreement crafted by the two sides’ lawyers.

Read More in Retail

The merchants opposing the settlement also contend that it is “riddled with loopholes that will make the relief largely ineffective.” Among those, the merchants say the settlement would allow “Visa and Mastercard to increase their network fees anytime ‘in response to market conditions.’”

The settlement also doesn’t preclude the networks from creating new types of merchant fees and that, because of the agreement’s liability release terms, would allow Visa and Mastercard legal immunity for any future fees they imposed, the 1,000-member merchant group wrote.

A Visa spokesperson declined to comment Monday on the merchants’ filings and pointed to a company statement when Cogan initially approved the settlement. “We believe the proposed settlement would provide U.S. merchants of all sizes with meaningful relief, more flexibility, and options to control how they accept payments from their customers,” Visa said in June.

A Mastercard spokesperson also nodded to the network’s comments from June that the “settlement agreement delivers on the expectations of the court and balances the interests of all parties involved.”

In their joint objection Monday, the National Retail Federation and the Retail Industry Leaders Association also cited constitutional “infirmities” with the pact.

The settlement “has traded true antitrust reforms that would apply competitive pressure to interchange fees for a series of half-measures that will yield varying, de minimis, or no benefit to millions. In return, it demands an incredibly broad release from a mandatory class with no right to opt out,” the retail groups wrote.

Some small businesses, including a convenience store and gas station, wrote to support the settlement.

Read More in Retail

“This agreement, which lowers swipe fees and gives businesses like mine more flexibility in how we accept cards and price around processing costs, would provide meaningful relief for an operation my size,” wrote Perry Patel, the owner of Tru Blue, a convenience store and gas station in Exmore, Virginia.

“Small businesses such as ours deserve every advantage available, and this settlement offers exactly that,” Ridge Fuller, owner of Big Daddy Automotive of Berryville, Virginia, wrote in an Aug. 27 letter. “It lowers costs to small businesses by reducing swipe fees without giving up the secure, dependable payment experience that make electronic payments a viable option.”

White House interest

Others found fault in the settlement. The FMI - The Food Industry Association, which represents food makers, grocers and pharmacies, said in its filing that the settlement “does not provide the meaningful relief from or permanent reform of the anticompetitive Visa-Mastercard duopoly that grocers have sought for over two decades.”

Last year, 42% of grocery purchases were made with a credit card, and 76% of all online grocery orders were paid with a credit card, according to data the association cited in its Aug. 28 letter from Stephanie Harris, chief public policy officer and general counsel.

In her letter, Harris also contrasted U.S. credit card fees with the European Union, which caps such fees at 0.3% per transaction, she wrote.

Debate over the settlement comes as President Donald Trump has been agitating this year for Congress to find a way to lower credit card fees, including pushing for passage of the Credit Card Competition Act.

The Republican president again mentioned the issue last week at his political convention in Dallas, while Vice President JD Vance brought up the Credit Card Competition Act on Monday while campaigning in Kansas for the bill’s Republican sponsor, Sen. Roger Marshall. Vance was a co-sponsor of the legislation when he was in the Senate, and called it “an issue that’s close to my heart.”

text:
USG Water Solutions has appointed Christina Coen as Chief Executive Officer, bringing in an executive with experience across water, specialty chemicals and business transformation as the company continues serving municipal water utilities across the United States.

Coen assumed the CEO role effective September 1, 2026, succeeding John Flaugher, who is transitioning to a strategic advisory position. The leadership change gives USG Water an executive with experience spanning operations, commercial strategy, research and development, sustainability and large-scale transformation.

USG Water provides water utility services focused on storage tanks, plant rehabilitation, metering and distribution systems. The company has more than 600 water utility maintenance professionals operating from 11 service centers and primarily serves rural and suburban communities and small cities across the country.

Coen joins the company from UPL Corp, where she most recently served as Chief Transformation Officer, R&D and Sustainability Lead. She previously served as Chief Marketing Officer at UPL with global profit-and-loss responsibility for a multi-billion-dollar portfolio.

Earlier in her career, Coen held senior leadership roles at Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, FMC Corporation and Dow Chemical. Her responsibilities across those organizations covered research and development, transformation, marketing and commercial leadership in water, agricultural and specialty chemical markets.

That combination of technical and commercial experience aligns with the operating requirements of USG Water, whose customers depend on maintaining aging and mission-critical infrastructure while meeting safety, quality and regulatory requirements.

“Our clients — rural and suburban communities and small cities across the country — depend on us to be true guardians of their water infrastructure,” Coen said. She identified continued investment in employees and technology as priorities while maintaining the company’s emphasis on safety, quality and compliance.

USG Water’s business addresses multiple components of utility infrastructure rather than a single maintenance category. Its services include work on water storage assets, treatment plants, metering infrastructure and distribution systems, allowing the company to support utilities across several areas of ongoing maintenance and rehabilitation.

The company’s geographic model also relies on locally positioned service teams. Its 11 service centers provide a base for more than 600 maintenance professionals who live and work in the communities and regions the company serves.

For smaller municipal and regional utilities, access to specialized maintenance capabilities can be particularly important because internal teams may not have the scale or technical resources to handle every rehabilitation, inspection, metering or distribution project themselves. USG Water’s service model is built around providing those capabilities across a broad customer base.

Coen’s background at Nalco Water gives her direct experience within the broader water industry, while her subsequent leadership positions add experience managing complex portfolios and organizational change. Her engineering training also provides a technical foundation relevant to an infrastructure services company.

She holds a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from Michigan State University and an MBA from Northwood University.

The transition of Flaugher into a strategic advisory role provides continuity as Coen assumes responsibility for the company’s operations and longer-term direction. USG Water did not disclose additional details about Flaugher’s advisory responsibilities.

Coen takes over a business with more than six decades of operating history and a national service footprint focused on essential municipal infrastructure. Her mandate will include maintaining that established service model while determining where additional technology, operational improvements and investment can strengthen the company’s capabilities.

As water utilities manage maintenance and rehabilitation needs across storage, treatment, metering and distribution assets, USG Water’s growth will depend on its ability to combine specialized field expertise with consistent execution across its service network. Coen’s appointment places an executive with both transformation and water-sector experience at the center of that effort.

name: Nvidia
title: Groq Navigates AI Cloud Market Shift After Nvidia Deal - Business Insider
description:
A $3.5 billion AI cloud with real infrastructure — and a harder fight to stand out without the signature chips that once made it a viable Nvidia challenger.
It was valued at $3.5 billion in its latest funding round, versus $6.9 billion before the Nvidia deal, though shareholders received payouts in between.
A 'mad dash' after the Nvidia deal When the Nvidia deal broke last December, Groq was thrown into limbo, former employees said.
Some Groq customers said it wasn't quite business as usual Some customers also felt friction.
Groq faces more AI competition Groq is fighting for customers as inference providers proliferate and become harder to distinguish.
text:
After Nvidia carved up much of Groq, the AI chip startup is now eyeing its next act.

So what's left? A $3.5 billion AI cloud with real infrastructure — and a harder fight to stand out without the signature chips that once made it a viable Nvidia challenger.

Last December, Nvidia paid roughly $20 billion to license Groq's signature chip architecture and hire its leadership, stopping short of a full acquisition. It was one of Nvidia's biggest deals ever and strengthened its position in inference — the fast-growing market for running AI models, where rivals have gained more ground than in training.

Groq 2.0 has lost some of what once made it stand out. Some customers said technical support and AI model choice worsened after the deal. And as inference becomes commoditized, price and speed increasingly matter more than which company provides it.

The unusual structure has also drawn scrutiny, with the Justice Department investigating whether it was designed to skirt antitrust review, The New York Times reported. Nvidia said in a statement that the deal was "the American system working as designed."

The surviving entity is hardly an empty shell. Groq has 13 data centers, plans to quadruple capacity next year, and 6 million developers and thousands of companies using its cloud. It's also increasingly relying on Nvidia systems — a striking reversal for a startup that once pitched its chips as a faster alternative.

Groq is backed by $1 billion in fresh capital. It was valued at $3.5 billion in its latest funding round, versus $6.9 billion before the Nvidia deal, though shareholders received payouts in between. It's betting on the sheer demand for AI compute.

"We think that the needs for inference are great," a source close to the company said. "It's sort of like the restaurant business. People just need food."

Nvidia said Groq "continues to be a separate and independent business."

A 'mad dash' after the Nvidia deal

When the Nvidia deal broke last December, Groq was thrown into limbo, former employees said. Management played the acquisition talks "very close to the vest," one said.

The deal came together in eight days, followed by a "mad dash" as former Groq employees became Nvidians overnight, a source close to the company said.

Groq quickly cycled through two CEOs. Simon Edwards, who had recently joined as chief financial officer, initially took over. Adam Winter assumed the helm in March, after which the company unveiled its new cloud-focused strategy.

Rather than walking away from its data-center commitments, Groq's leadership quickly realized it could refit the sites with Nvidia hardware, a source close to the company said.

The deal reshaped Groq's workforce. Most of the hardware and software engineering teams — including the majority of the cloud engineering team that built GroqCloud — moved to Nvidia, while data center operations, legal, human resources, finance, and other business functions largely remained to keep the entity running. The company has since added cloud and infrastructure veterans to its C-suite.

The upheaval didn't mean employees walked away empty-handed. Those who held equity received payouts from the deal, according to two former employees.

Some Groq customers said it wasn't quite business as usual

Some customers also felt friction.

Before the deal, the company had been known for a "very, very hands-on" approach to customer support, a third former employee said.

Paul Richards, cofounder and CEO of the AI startup Recall, said uncertainty about Groq's future prompted it to rely less on the company and work with other providers — though roughly a quarter of its inference still runs on Groq.

"Every person I spoke to there left the company. So that obviously was alarming," he said.

Recall previously had a private Slack with Groq employees, Richards said, and after the deal, "it was crickets."

Richards also said that Groq discontinued many of the AI models Recall used and wasn't adding the newer models he requested.

Willow cofounder Lawrence Liu saw key support staff move to Nvidia, requiring a "re-initiation period" with their replacements, though the transition was quick and the service remained reliable.

ScreenApp CEO Andre Dean Smith said Groq fell behind on some model updates and never delivered a planned feature. That prompted his company to shift work elsewhere, though it has since expanded its use of Groq again, he said.

A source close to Groq said that while customers may have lost support contacts who moved to Nvidia, they were connected with replacements, and no complaints reached leadership.

Not everyone noticed the disruption. Eoin McMillan, founder of Sourcetable, said it was "business as usual" after the deal.

"From my end user experience, you would never know anything happened at all," he said.

Groq faces more AI competition

Groq is fighting for customers as inference providers proliferate and become harder to distinguish. Its rivals span inference specialists like Fireworks and Together AI, neoclouds such as CoreWeave, and cloud giants like Amazon and Google.

Groq says it has unique experience running its AI chips, known as language processing units, at scale, and that it will be among the first to deploy Nvidia's latest inference systems that incorporate them.

"You've got a billion-dollar-financed inference-native cloud," said early Groq investor David Levy of Porch Capital. "Shouldn't this be a big deal? I think it is."

The harder question is what will make customers choose Groq. Speed gaps are narrowing. And companies like OpenRouter make it easier for developers to switch between AI providers.

"Economics is the best thing they can offer their customers," said Ashish Nadkarni, an IDC vice president focused on enterprise infrastructure.

Sourcetable's McMillan said that Groq's speed once made it an obvious choice for certain workloads. Since then, competing services have gotten fast enough to narrow the advantage.

Groq doesn't see that as a problem. Demand is high enough to mint multiple winners, a source close to the company said: "You don't necessarily need a moat."

description:

This includes Generative Media Tool, which allows editors to generate video and sound effects directly in the timeline.

text:
Adobe has added generative AI tools directly into its Premiere and After Effects platforms.

This includes Generative Media Tool, which allows editors to generate video and sound effects directly in the timeline. Users select Generative Media, describe what they want and where they want it, and Premiere then generates context-aware, fully editable video and audio clips. These can use Adobe’s Firefly AI models, as well as partner models including Google Veo, Kling, Runway and Luma.

In addition to videos and sound effects, there is Generate Soundscape and Generate Music, both in beta. Soundscape analyses up to 15 seconds of video to automatically generate contextually informed audio with layers of ambience and sound effects customised and timed to their edit, while Music can generate original music with multiple variations to choose from, with controls for tempo and looping. Generated music is commercially safe, with synchronisation rights across any type of media.

Previously, editors would have had to leave Premiere and use Adobe Firefly, before round-tripping content back to Premiere, to use these kinds of tools.

There have also been a number of AI-powered audio tools brought into Premiere, including a public beta of Enhance Audio. This builds on the Enhance Speech tool already in the editing software, and gives control over dialogue, music, ambience and sound effects within a single clip, so users can remove elements, adjust layers or mute dialogue entirely.

There are also tools to separate crosstalk, Dynamic Auto Ducking to automatically balance different elements, and more.

For After Effects, Adobe has added an AI assistant that has the power to complete tasks. Now in beta, AI Assistant can work across an entire project, with users describing what they want it to do in natural language.

Tasks could include reorganising large projects with thousands of layers, repairing and solving technical issues, and creating sophisticated motion effects like expressions without needing to write code. It can also execute tasks based on direction like inspecting compositions and footage.

text:
A phase 2 trial of Johnson & Johnson’s JNJ-5120 has missed its primary endpoint, denting the prospects of the Contineum Therapeutics-partnered depression drug candidate.

In 2023, J&J paid Pipeline Therapeutics $50 million upfront and committed up to $1 billion in milestones for global rights to the M1 receptor antagonist, which is also called PIPE-307. Pipeline, which rebranded as Contineum later in 2023, had completed two phase 1 trials of the drug candidate, teeing J&J up to run midphase studies in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) and major depressive disorder (MDD).

Ten months after disclosing the failure of the MS trial, Contineum reported that the MDD study missed its primary endpoint. Investigators randomized 107 people with MDD to receive one of two JNJ-5120 regimens or placebo.

At Day 5, patients receiving JNJ-5120 performed no better on a depression scale than those on placebo, causing the trial to miss its primary endpoint. William Blair analysts removed JNJ-5120 from their model in response to the setback, extinguishing hopes of success that they had put at 35% before the readout.

“We had always viewed the study as risky, especially considering the risky nature of placebo-controlled studies in MDD, where placebo responses have eroded effect sizes and patient heterogeneity can lead to volatility in patient response rates on active drug,” the analysts said.

J&J has yet to give up on the asset. The Big Pharma continues to evaluate the results, including data on prespecified exploratory endpoints, Contineum said. J&J’s review of the totality and clinical relevance of its findings will inform the next steps.

Investors appeared sanguine about the setback, sending Contineum’s share price down just 3.5% to $14.30 in after-hours trading. The muted response aligns with the assessment of William Blair analysts, who said most of Contineum’s value is tied to the LPAR1 antagonist, PIPE-791, which the company is developing in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

PIPE-791, a potential rival to Bristol Myers Squibb’s admilparant, is in phase 2 development. The next key catalyst for Contineum's shares is readthrough from phase 3 data on admilparant, which BMS is expected to share early in the fourth quarter, the analysts said.

text:
Highlights

An interim dividend is scheduled for payment on 14 September 2026

Pearson has been shifting its business mix toward digital learning and professional certification

Traditional print textbook revenue has declined as a share of the group's overall earnings

Pearson has spent recent years shifting its business mix away from traditional print textbooks toward digital learning platforms, professional certification and workforce skills products. That transition has changed the underlying growth and margin drivers behind the group's earnings, and by extension its dividend capacity.

The interim payment reflects earnings generated across this evolving mix, with digital and services revenue increasingly central to the investment case relative to the group's legacy print publishing business.

How Pearson Fits The Sector

Within communication stocks, Pearson is grouped with other UK-listed information and publishing names, though its focus on education and professional certification distinguishes it from broader business information peers.

Professional Certification As A Growth Area

Growth in professional testing and certification services has been highlighted by management as a key area of focus, offering a different demand profile from the more cyclical education publishing markets Pearson has traditionally served.

Placing This In The Wider Communication Stocks Picture

Pearson (LSE:PSON) Communication Services Pearson PLC (LSE:PSON) 1187.00 GBX -4.500 ↓ 0.378% sits within the communication stocks segment of the London market, and investors following Communication Stocks often track its digital transition as an example of how information and publishing businesses are adapting business models across the sector.

What Investors Should Watch From Here

Digital revenue growth, professional certification volumes and further declines in legacy FTSE 100 print publishing are the main factors likely to shape future dividend decisions.

The September payment continues Pearson's established approach to shareholder returns through its ongoing business transition.

Dividend Tax Considerations For UK Investors

Dividend income received outside a tax-efficient wrapper is generally subject to UK dividend tax once it exceeds an annual tax-free allowance, with the rate charged depending on which income tax band the dividend falls into. These allowances and rates are reviewed periodically by HMRC, so investors should check current thresholds rather than rely on prior-year figures when estimating their own liability.

Holding shares like Pearson within an ISA or a SIPP shelters dividend income from this tax entirely, which is one reason many UK income investors prioritise using their tax-efficient allowances before holding dividend payers in a general investment account. This is general information rather than personal tax advice, and investors with specific questions about their own position should speak to a qualified adviser.

Currency And Overseas Earnings Exposure

Companies that generate a significant share of revenue or profit outside the UK can see their dividend capacity, and the sterling value of any payment, affected by currency movements even when the underlying business performance is stable. A stronger pound relative to the currencies a company earns in can reduce the sterling-equivalent value of profits and dividends, while a weaker pound can boost it.

This dynamic is relevant for Pearson to the extent its earnings are generated outside the UK, and investors following communication stocks more broadly often keep an eye on relevant exchange rates alongside underlying operational performance when assessing future dividend prospects.

Understanding Dividend Cover And Payout Sustainability

Dividend cover, calculated by dividing a company's earnings per share by its dividend per share, is one of the simplest ways investors assess whether a payout looks sustainable. A cover ratio comfortably above one suggests a business is generating more profit than it distributes, leaving room to absorb a difficult year without cutting the dividend. A ratio close to or below one, by contrast, can signal that a payout is being funded from reserves or borrowing rather than current earnings, which tends to draw closer scrutiny from income-focused shareholders.

For Pearson, as with any communication stocks constituent, dividend cover is best read alongside free cash flow generation and balance sheet strength rather than in isolation, since accounting profit and cash profit can diverge meaningfully depending on the business model. Investors tracking the interim dividend typically watch subsequent results releases for management commentary on cover and cash generation, since that context often shapes expectations for future payments.

Tracking Pearson's Dividend Calendar

Company announcements, known as RNS releases in the UK, are the primary source for dividend declarations, confirming the amount, the ex-dividend date, the record date and the payment date for each distribution. Most brokers also maintain a dividend calendar tool that aggregates this information across an investor's holdings.

For those following Pearson specifically, the company's own investor relations page typically lists historical and upcoming dividend dates, alongside results announcements that often accompany or precede a new declaration.

How Dividend Dates Work: Declaration, Ex-Dividend And Payment

Every dividend moves through a predictable sequence of dates. The declaration date is when the board formally announces the payout and its amount. The ex-dividend date follows, marking the cut-off after which new buyers of the shares are no longer entitled to that specific payment; the shares typically trade lower by roughly the dividend amount on that day, all else being equal. The record date confirms which shareholders are on the register to receive payment, and the payment date is when the cash actually lands in accounts.

Investors interested in qualifying for Pearson's interim dividend need to own the shares before the ex-dividend date, not simply before the payment date, a distinction that catches out some newer income investors. Brokers and the London Stock Exchange's own announcements are the most reliable places to confirm the exact dates for any individual payment.

OpenAI acquired Glass Imaging, a startup developing AI-powered smartphone camera technology, in a deal valued at over $300 million, according to The Wall Street Journal. The purchase price represents a significant jump from the roughly $100 million valuation Glass Imaging carried in a funding round last year.

Glass Imaging was founded in 2019 by Ziv Attar and Tom Bishop, two former Apple engineers who worked on the company's Portrait Mode feature. The Los Altos, California-based company had raised about $30 million from investors including GV, Alphabet's venture arm, and Insight Partners before the acquisition.

Glass Imaging's approach differs from conventional AI photo editing: instead of processing images after the fact, the company teaches neural networks the specific optical properties of each camera system so that picture quality is improved as the shot is taken, according to The Wall Street Journal. The company's goal is to produce image quality comparable to a DSLR camera from a smartphone. Its zoom-imaging technology was featured in a line of phones from Chinese smartphone brand Honor.

OpenAI's plans for Glass Imaging are unclear. The company is also developing a device with Jony Ive, the former Apple designer behind the iPhone. OpenAI brought on Ive in 2025 through its $6.5 billion purchase of io Products, and his responsibilities span hardware development alongside broader efforts to define how AI products will look and function.

text:
FRANKFURT/MILAN, Sept 15 (Reuters) - UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel does not want Bettina Orlopp to remain as Commerzbank CEO and is opposed to Berlin keeping two supervisory board seats, three people with knowledge of the matter said, as he moves towards taking over the German bank.

UniCredit also wants Commerzbank Chairman Jens Weidmann to leave, two of the people said.

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil and Orcel met on Monday on the Italian bank's takeover plans, a turning point in the two-year battle for control of one of Germany's biggest banks after Berlin failed in its attempt to stymie a takeover. Both called the meeting "constructive."

UniCredit did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for Commerzbank dismissed any changes in management, saying "The board of Commerzbank AG has running contracts, the supervisory board is elected by the general assembly, and there's full alignment on strategy."

Germany's finance ministry declined to comment further, after saying on Monday it wants to keep two board seats.

It was unclear if the leadership roles or UniCredit's opposition to the German government maintaining two board seats were discussed at Monday's meeting in Berlin.

"We are currently represented on Commerzbank's supervisory board and will continue to be," Klingbeil told reporters on Tuesday, adding: "And, naturally, if and when the time comes, we also expect to be represented on UniCredit's board".

NEW SHAREHOLDER REPRESENTATIVES

Orlopp said last month she was not feeling pressure to give up her role after the months-long ownership battle over Germany's second-largest bank, which both the Commerzbank CEO and Weidmann have said should remain independent.

Orcel repeatedly said over the summer he wanted to engage with Commerzbank employee representatives, local authorities and central government, leaving out Orlopp and Weidmann. UniCredit is in a position to call an extraordinary shareholder meeting and appoint new shareholder representatives at Commerzbank, he said.

Germany won the right to appoint two board members when it rescued Commerzbank in 2009 during the global financial crisis.

It retains a stake of 13.3% and it is not clear how UniCredit could block Berlin retaining two members while it remains a shareholder.

In addition to the board seats, Berlin has set out a number of other demands relating to a UniCredit takeover, including Commerzbank remaining listed on the stock exchange, keeping its base in Frankfurt and continuing to finance German medium-sized companies at home and abroad.

After months of resistance, German government officials and Commerzbank executives softened their stance on a potential deal after UniCredit amassed a stake of nearly 50%.

Now German officials are hoping to protect jobs as well as the brand of a bank that plays a critical role in financing the medium-sized companies in Europe's largest economy, whose government is in the throes of a political crisis.

A combination of UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than EUR1.3 trillion in assets across two of the euro zone's largest economies.

(Reporting by Tom Sims and Valentina Za; additional reporting by Maria Martinez and Christian Kraemer; editing by Friederike Heine and Alexander Smith)

text:
Nvidia and Palantir announced on Thursday that they will incorporate an artificial intelligence model into the control of their critical supply chains, giving the automated system decision-making power.

"Nvidia has arguably the most valuable, intricate, and complex supply chain in the world. Our sovereign stack, powered by Nemotron models and Ontology, is delivering capabilities that exceed the frontier while providing alpha protection qualities unavailable otherwise,” said Alex Karp, cofounder and CEO of Palantir Technologies.

The deployment, according to the companies, will allow for "unprecedented supply chain visibility, identify constraints, continuously codify operational expertise and guide decisions at machine speed."

The system will be first implemented in Nvidia's supply chain, which spans millions of parts, thousands of suppliers, and a global network of manufacturing partners, with the objective of unifying every team worldwide into one operating system that improves their efficiency.

"Supply chains are the operating system of the physical economy, and AI factories are among the most complex systems ever built,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia. “From wafers and components to manufacturing, systems and customer delivery, hundreds of companies and trillions of dollars of global economic activity come together to deliver AI infrastructure. NVIDIA and Palantir are transforming this vast operational graph into sovereign intelligence."

The human side is still key for the system

Even if Nvidia reported that planners improved their numbers when using the new model, it also said human employees still provided key insights that weren't possible to get using only an AI system.

According to the company, emails exchanged with partners that week, severe weather in the forecast for a key region, an ongoing geopolitical event, or understanding the transcript from the last supplier debrief call were factors the AI struggled to incorporate when working across the entire supply chain.

The company explained that those inputs were better implemented by human instinct created by years of work rather than by the mathematical algorithm that guided the system, while the AI had an important role in working around the repetitive and predictable tasks.

The company concluded that the best implementation would help workers spend less time reconstructing routine decisions so they could focus on unpredictable situations.

Additionally, the Nvidia explained that the model was only going to train according to insights provided by the workers, with no changes made during production while managing a supply chain.

text:
OpenAI has been signaling for months that it wants a bigger foothold in the legal industry. A new partnership offers a clue as to how it plans to get there: not just by selling models and software, but by sending people to help customers actually use them.

Telon, a London startup, is one of the companies giving it boots on the ground.

Rather than sell software, Telon hires and trains "legal engineers" — mostly former lawyers who embed inside law firms and corporate legal teams to help them get more out of the tech they already buy. The model is a bit like forward-deployed engineering-as-a-service.

The startup isn't six months old yet, and it already has the attention of a tech goliath. Telon said Tuesday that OpenAI named it a "select partner," a role that will have the startup working with shared customers to configure models, write prompts, build agents, and train lawyers.

The ChatGPT maker launched the OpenAI Partner Network in June to make it easier for consultants and other partners to bring its models and software into companies around the world. OpenAI said it aims to certify 300,000 consultants by the end of 2026.

Lewis Bretts, a former trial attorney, built up PwC's legal practice before founding Telon in June. He said the hardest part about selling artificial intelligence to law firms isn't closing the deal. It's getting lawyers to actually use it.

That pain point has created a growing line of business for professional services firms, which have long helped companies adopt enterprise software. Bretts said he started Telon after noticing a change in how that work gets done.

Enterprises once hired firms like McKinsey or Deloitte to roll out a Salesforce database or another large tech system — a project that might take months or years, but eventually ended.

AI is different. Labs ship new models all the time. Each release expands what the apps built on top can do. A company can buy licenses and run a successful pilot, Bretts said, only to find months later that employees are using a fraction of what the technology can do.

Telon is betting there is room for a legal specialist to close that gap. Since June, the company has grown to 30 team members and raised capital from Zach Posner's LegalTech Fund. Bretts declined to name customers or disclose the financial terms of its OpenAI agreement.

The partnership gives Telon a stamp of credibility.

It may help OpenAI answer a harder question, too.

The company is pushing deeper into legal work, but its pitch runs up against a familiar refrain: Why should a law firm buy directly from a model provider when specialized app companies build around the way lawyers actually work?

Telon might give OpenAI a way to borrow some of that niche.
